summary: Specifies Wave and Equation Based Rate Control (WEBRC), a congestion control building block for IP multicast. Receivers join the same session at different rates depending on their connections, and no feedback to the sender is needed because it is receiver-driven. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3738 defines WEBRC, a way to keep a multicast session from overwhelming the network. Each receiver works out its own sending rate from the packet loss and delay it measures, and adjusts by joining and leaving channels. The sender never receives any feedback, so the scheme scales to very large numbers of receivers.

subtitle: Congestion control for multicast where every receiver sets its own rate and the sender never hears back.

tldr.problem: A multicast sender cannot ask each receiver how fast it should send, because a session may have a very large number of receivers and feedback from all of them would not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The sender transmits the session over several channels with staggered sending rates. Each receiver measures its own loss and its own multicast round-trip time, computes a target rate from a TCP-like equation, and joins or leaves channels to move its own rate towards that target.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental building block, published while the Reliable Multicast Transport Working Group waited for deployment experience before re-submitting it as a Proposed Standard. The memo describes it as reasonably fair to TCP but slower to react to a change in bandwidth.

today: RFC 3738 is an Experimental document from April 2004, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo records that the Reliable Multicast Transport Working Group published it in the Experimental category while waiting for deployment and experience, with the intention of re-submitting it as a Proposed Standard once the scheme was judged adequate.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
WEBRC is a congestion control building block designed to be massively scalable when used with the IP multicast network service. It is also suitable as the basis for unicast congestion control, though that is outside the scope of the memo. It is designed to compete fairly with TCP and similar congestion-controlled sessions, and it can be used as the congestion control protocol for any type of data delivery, including reliable content delivery and streaming delivery.

WEBRC is a receiver-driven congestion control protocol. All the measurements and all the decisions to raise or lower the reception rate are made by each individual receiver, and those decisions are acted on by sending join and leave messages for channels to the network. A receiver adjusts its reception rate without regard to other concerns such as reliability, which differs from TCP, where the congestion control protocol and the reliability protocol are intricately interwoven. WEBRC takes the same equation-based approach as TFRC: each receiver measures parameters that are plugged into a TCP-like equation to compute a target reception rate, then adjusts its rate up and down to approximate that target.

The sender sends packets to multiple channels. One is the base channel and the rest are wave channels. Each wave channel follows the same pattern of packet rate transmission spread over equally spaced intervals of time, and the pattern of each wave is that it starts at a high rate and the rate decreases gradually and continually over a long period. A receiver raises its rate by joining the next wave channel earlier in the descent of the wave than it joined the previous one, and lowers its rate by joining the next wave channel later in the descent.

The memo introduces a multicast round-trip time, written MRTT. Each receiver measures one individually and averages it as a substitute for the conventional unicast round-trip time, because the throughput of a TCP session depends strongly on round-trip time, so some measure of it is needed for the equation to be TCP-friendly. Using the MRTT also helps to coordinate and equalize the reception rates of proximate receivers joined to a session behind a bottleneck link, which means packets flowing through that link are on average sent to almost all downstream receivers, so the efficiencies of multicast are realized.

WEBRC is designed to be reasonably fair when competing for bandwidth with TCP flows, where a flow is reasonably fair if its reception rate is generally within a factor of two of the reception rate of a TCP flow under the same conditions. Its throughput varies less over time than TCP's, which suits telephony and streaming media, but the penalty for that smoothness is that WEBRC responds more slowly than TCP to changes in available bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem with multicast is scale: a sender cannot poll every viewer. WEBRC solves this by letting each viewer decide its own rate from what it observes locally, and by giving the sender nothing to read. The result is smooth and fair to TCP, but slower to react when the network changes.

sections.title: Sessions, Channels and Waves
sections.content:
A WEBRC session is a logically related set of channels from a single sender, used for some period of time to carry data packets whose header carries WEBRC Congestion Control Information. Received packets are first checked to see that they belong to the right session before WEBRC is applied, and how that filtering is done is outside the scope of the memo. A channel is uniquely identified at the network layer by a pair of sender IP address and multicast group address, and that is the address a receiver sends join and leave messages to. The channels of a session map uniquely to consecutive channel numbers, and each packet carries the channel number of its channel in the Congestion Control Information.

At the sender, time is partitioned into time slots of duration TSD seconds, and there are a fixed number T of time slot indices in a session. The current time slot index increases by one modulo T each TSD seconds and is carried in every packet, which lets receivers synchronize coarsely within a session. Congestion control works because the sender sends a session's packets to several different channels and receivers join and leave those channels according to the congestion they experience, each receiver acting independently of all the others and with no impact on the sender.

The channels of a session are one base channel and T wave channels. For the base channel, packets are sent at a low rate BCR_P at the beginning of a time slot and the rate decreases gradually to P times BCR_P at the end of the time slot, where P is less than 1, and this pattern repeats in each time slot. For each wave channel, packets are sent at a rate that first increases very quickly to a high rate and then decreases by a fixed fraction P per time slot until it reaches BCR_P at the end of the time slot. Then the channel is quiescent for a period, and the whole cycle repeats, with a duration of T times TSD seconds.

The active wave channels are ordered into layers at each point in time. The lowest layer is the active wave channel whose wave is nearest completion, and the highest layer is the one furthest from completion. Each time a wave channel becomes active it is the highest layer, and at the end of each time slot the lowest-layer wave channel becomes quiescent and the others move down a layer. At each point in time a receiver is joined to the base channel and to a consecutive set of layers starting at the lowest, and it always leaves the lowest layer when that layer becomes quiescent.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is split across several channels. One channel carries a low, steadily falling rate and lets receivers keep their clocks in step. The other channels each carry a burst that starts fast and fades away. A receiver picks up more or less of these bursts to set its own speed.

sections.title: Sender Operation
sections.content:
The sender operation is by design much simpler than the receiver operation. Its primary input is SR_b, an upper bound on the sender's transmission rate in bits per second at any point in time, in aggregate across all channels. It is RECOMMENDED that this aggregate rate be constant, and that the session description say whether it is. The secondary inputs are the packet length LENP_B, which should be set as high as possible without exceeding the MTU of the network that would cause fragmentation; BCR_P, the transmission rate on the base channel at the beginning of a time slot in packets per second, whose default value is 1; TSD, the time slot duration in seconds, for which the RECOMMENDED value is 10; QD, the minimum quiescent period in seconds, for which the RECOMMENDED value is 300; P, the multiplicative drop in every channel rate over each time slot, whose default value is 0.75; and N, the duration in time slots of each wave, which is also the number of wave channels active at any time.

From these the sender derives fixed parameters: the transmission rate in packets per second, the base channel rate in bits per second, the number of base channel packets sent in each time slot, the number of quiescent time slots per cycle, the total number of time slots in a cycle, which is also the total number of wave channels, and the total duration of a cycle in seconds.

For each packet the sender places the current time slot index and the channel number of the channel into the Congestion Control Information, and calculates a packet sequence number that is scoped by the channel number and increases consecutively within each channel. For each wave channel the last packet sent before the channel becomes quiescent must carry the maximum possible sequence number, which is 65,535 in the short format and 4,294,967,295 in the long format. For the base channel, the first packet of each time slot has a sequence number congruent to zero modulo the number of base channel packets per slot.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender does very little beyond keeping to a schedule. Each packet says which time slot it belongs to, which channel it went out on, and its position in that channel's sequence, so receivers can work out what they missed.

sections.title: What the Receiver Measures and Computes
sections.content:
The receiver keeps a target reception rate at all times and may join the next wave channel if the rate it would reach by joining does not exceed that target. The target is continually updated from two primary measurements: an estimate of the average loss probability, and an estimate of the average multicast round-trip time. Both are moving averages of measurements taken at discrete events. The loss estimate applies two exponentially weighted moving average filters to the packet reception measurements, one time-based and one loss-based, with recommended smoothing constants of 0.3 for each. The time-based filter exists because loss events in WEBRC are bursty, typically occurring just after a new wave has been joined.

The receiver computes the reception rate from the TCP equation, using the average round-trip time and the estimated loss probability. It makes its join decisions at equally spaced intervals called epochs, whose duration EL is set to a small fraction of the time slot duration, with a standard setting of EL equal to TSD divided by 20. It maintains two averaged reception rates: the true reception rate, used in start-up mode and for setting the slow start rate, and the anticipated reception rate, which estimates the total instantaneous rate of the channels it is joined to and is the value compared against the target rate.

A slow start mechanism lets the rate ramp up quickly at the start of a session and after a sudden drop. It keeps a minimum slow start threshold rate and a slow start threshold rate that starts at infinity, so that the receiver does not try to compute a meaningful target rate from its measurements before it has any. The start-up period ends when a packet loss is detected, when a sharp increase in the multicast round-trip time is detected, when the maximum reception rate is reached, or when the true reception rate is not rising consistently with the last join of a wave channel. In typical operation the target rate is the minimum of the maximum of the slow start threshold and the rate from the TCP equation, and the receiver's own maximum rate; while the slow start threshold is still infinite the target rate is four times the true reception rate, capped by the same maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver watches two things: how many packets it is losing, and how long the round trip is taking. It feeds those into the same kind of formula TCP uses, and then moves towards the result by joining or leaving channels. At the start it climbs quickly, then settles into a steady rate.

sections.title: The Congestion Control Information Fields
sections.content:
Packets sent to a session using WEBRC MUST include Congestion Control Information fields. The memo specifies a short and a long format, and recommends that protocol instantiations use one of them. Other formats may be used, but every instantiation is REQUIRED to use a format compatible with the interpretation of these fields, and a protocol that uses a different format MUST specify the lengths and positions of the fields within its packet header. All integer fields are carried in big-endian, or network order, format.

The short format is 32 bits long and holds three fields. The Current Time Slot Index takes 8 bits and indicates the index of the current time slot, increasing by one modulo T each TSD seconds at the sender. Since T is also the number of wave channels, T must be at most 255. The Channel Number takes 8 bits and is the number of the channel the packet belongs to, with the base channel numbered T and the wave channels numbered 0 to T minus 1, so T plus 1 channels are used in total and T must be at most 255. The Packet Sequence Number takes 16 bits and is scoped by its channel number value, numbered consecutively modulo 2 to the 16 within each cycle and ending with the last packet sent to a wave channel before that channel goes quiescent, which carries the value 2 to the 16 minus 1.

The long format is 64 bits long and means the same thing, with each field twice as long: a 16-bit Current Time Slot Index, a 16-bit Channel Number, and a 32-bit Packet Sequence Number numbered modulo 2 to the 32 and ending at 2 to the 32 minus 1. With the long format, T must be at most 65,535.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet carries three numbers: which time slot it belongs to, which channel it went out on, and its position in that channel's sequence. The short form fits in 32 bits and the long form in 64 bits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
WEBRC can be subject to denial-of-service attacks by attackers who try to confuse the congestion control mechanism for receivers by injecting forged packets into the multicast stream. The attack most adversely affects network elements and receivers downstream of the attack, and much less significantly the rest of the network and other receivers. Because of this, and because of the potential attacks from the use of forward error correction, it is RECOMMENDED that Reverse Path Forwarding checks be enabled in all network routers and switches along the path from the sender to receivers, to limit the possibility of a bad agent injecting forged packets into the multicast tree data path.

The memo also notes that source authentication schemes such as TESLA could be used to authenticate packets and, for example, to terminate the session on detecting a forged packet. It RECOMMENDED that the normal receiver responses to received packets happen immediately rather than being delayed by the authentication process, because the overall performance would be greatly degraded if the receiver delayed its response for several seconds.

Two further risks are named. A receiver with an incorrect or corrupted implementation may affect the health of the network in the path and the reception rates of other receivers, so it is RECOMMENDED that receivers be required to identify themselves as legitimate before they receive the session description they need to join. And a receiver may obtain an incorrect session description, which would leave legitimate receivers unable to receive the content or might make receivers try to receive at a much higher rate than they can manage, disrupting traffic in parts of the network. To avoid this, it is RECOMMENDED that measures be taken to prevent receivers from accepting incorrect session descriptions, for example by using source authentication so that receivers only accept descriptions from authorized senders.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who can inject fake packets into a multicast stream can push receivers into sending too fast, which is a denial of service. The memo recommends checking the source address of packets along the path, and warns that a receiver with a broken implementation or a wrong session description can also disturb the network.

items.title: Receiver-driven
items.text: Each receiver makes its own measurements and its own rate decisions.

items.title: No feedback
items.text: The sender never learns what the receivers are doing.

items.title: Multiple rate
items.text: Receivers joined to one session can receive at different rates.

items.title: Reasonably fair to TCP
items.text: Within a factor of two of a TCP flow's rate under the same conditions.

items.title: Smooth
items.text: Less variation of throughput over time than TCP, which suits streaming.

items.title: Slow to react
items.text: Responds more slowly than TCP to a change in available bandwidth.

fields.desc: Position within the channel, numbered consecutively modulo 2^16 and ending at 65,535 before a wave channel goes quiescent.
